(CNN) -- Three former guerrilla leaders -- who helped command what one activist called "one of the most brutal rebel movements in modern days" -- were sentenced Wednesday in Freetown, Sierra Leone, for crimes against humanity. Amputee victims of Sierra Leone's civil war take part in football training at a beach in Freetown. The U.N. Special Court for Sierra Leone found the men guilty in February of crimes that included murder, rape, sexual slavery and forced marriages stemming from a civil war that lasted from March 1991 to January 2002. They were arrested in March 2003, said Peter Anderson, spokesman for the U.N. court. The rebels -- former leaders in the Revolutionary United Front guerrilla movement -- were known for hacking off civilians' hands and feet during the war, which stood out for its viciousness even on a a continent that has suffered many horrific conflicts. Presiding Judge Pierre Boutet of Canada read the sentences. Former Revolutionary United Front "interim leader" Issa Hassan Sesay was sentenced to 52 years in prison, former commander Morris Kallon to 40 years, and former chief of security Augustine Gbao to 25 years. Sesay and Kallon had been found guilty on 16 counts, and Gbao was found guilty on 14. The former rebels received credit for the six years each already has served in prison, Anderson told CNN. He said they will be imprisoned in another country, maybe Rwanda, because the prisons in Sierra Leone do not meet the standards of the U.N. court. Kallon was the only one of the three to express sorrow at his sentencing, Anderson said. "He really had made a genuine expression of remorse," which is considered a stronger statement than regret, the court spokesman added. The court noted several mitigating factors at the sentencing, but "in view of the gravity of the crimes, their impact was limited," a statement from the court said. The court noted that the crimes "were committed upon a massive scale across several districts of Sierra Leone" and that "the impact of all these crimes upon the Sierra Leonean society has been enormous." "The Chamber concluded that the inherent gravity of the criminal acts for which Sesay, Kallon and Gbao have been convicted is exceptionally high," the statement said. Corinne Dufka, a senior researcher in Human Rights Watch's Africa division, had called the verdict "very significant." "The RUF were renowned for leading one of the most brutal rebel movements in modern days. Everyone knows about the signature atrocity of limb amputation, but there was also horrific sexual violence, abductions, use of child soldiers and forced marriages," she told CNN by phone from Senegal in West Africa. The three had pleaded not guilty on all counts. The Special Court cannot impose the death penalty. The Revolutionary United Front seized most of Sierra Leone from the government and fought international and African peacekeepers. International forces retook the capital, Freetown, in 2000. The prosecution rested in the Taylor case in January after a year of presenting its arguments. The Special Court is an independent tribunal established jointly by the United Nations and the Sierra Leone government. # U.N. Court Sentences Three Former RUF Leaders for Crimes Against Humanity

**FREETOWN, Sierra Leone** — Three former leaders of the notorious Revolutionary United Front were sentenced to decades in prison Wednesday by a U.N.-backed court, marking a significant milestone in efforts to hold accountable those responsible for atrocities committed during Sierra Leone's brutal civil war.

The Special Court for Sierra Leone handed down sentences ranging from 25 to 52 years to the three men, who were convicted of multiple counts of crimes against humanity and war crimes, including murder, rape, sexual slavery, and the conscription of child soldiers.

Issa Sesay, considered the most senior of the three defendants, received the harshest sentence. Morris Kallon and Augustine Gbao received lengthy prison terms as well, according to court officials.

## A Legacy of Terror

The Revolutionary United Front waged a decade-long insurgency against successive Sierra Leonean governments beginning in 1991. The conflict became infamous worldwide for its extreme brutality, particularly the group's signature practice of hacking off the hands, arms, and legs of civilians, including women and children.

The war, which killed an estimated 50,000 people and displaced millions, was fueled in part by the illicit trade in so-called "blood diamonds" — precious stones mined in conflict zones and sold to finance the fighting.

"This judgment sends a clear message that those who commit such heinous acts will be held accountable," a court spokesperson said following the sentencing. "There can be no impunity for crimes of this magnitude."

## Landmark Convictions

Legal observers noted the significance of the verdicts, particularly the convictions related to forced marriage and the use of child soldiers, which set important precedents in international criminal law.

The Special Court, established jointly by the United Nations and the government of Sierra Leone in 2002, was created specifically to prosecute those bearing "the greatest responsibility" for atrocities committed during the conflict.

## Reaction and Reflection

For many Sierra Leoneans, the sentencing brought a measure of justice, though the wounds of the war remain deep. Survivors and human rights advocates who gathered to hear the verdict expressed a mix of relief and lingering grief.

Human rights organizations praised the outcome as an important step, while emphasizing that continued support for victims and reconciliation efforts would be essential to healing the nation.

The convictions come as part of broader international efforts to address war crimes committed during the West African nation's civil war, which formally ended in 2002.

Defense attorneys for the men indicated they were reviewing the decision and considering their options for appeal.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

## Landmark Verdict Marks Accountability for Brutal Civil War Atrocities

The Special Court for Sierra Leone handed down significant prison sentences to three former commanders of the Revolutionary United Front (RUF), concluding one of the most important war crimes trials stemming from the country's devastating civil war that ravaged the West African nation from 1991 to 2002.

## The Sentences

The court convicted and sentenced the three defendants as follows:

- **Issa Hassan Sesay**, the RUF's interim leader, received a sentence of **52 years** in prison
- **Morris Kallon**, a senior RUF commander, was sentenced to **40 years**
- **Augustine Gbao**, the RUF's security chief, received a **25-year** sentence

These sentences, delivered in 2009, represented some of the most substantial penalties issued by the tribunal.

## The Charges

The three men were found guilty on multiple counts encompassing a wide range of atrocities committed during the conflict, including:

- **Murder and extermination**
- **Rape and sexual slavery**
- **Mutilation and amputation** of civilians—a signature horror of the conflict in which victims had limbs hacked off
- **Recruitment and use of child soldiers**
- **Enslavement and forced labor**
- **Attacks against United Nations peacekeepers**

Notably, the case marked the first time an international tribunal secured convictions for forced marriage as a crime against humanity, and the first convictions for attacks against UN peacekeeping personnel.

## Background to the Conflict

The Sierra Leone civil war was characterized by extreme brutality, particularly the RUF's practice of amputating the hands, arms, and legs of civilians, including children. The conflict claimed an estimated 50,000 lives and displaced millions, while thousands more were left permanently maimed. The war became notorious internationally for its connection to "blood diamonds," which financed the fighting.

## Significance of the Verdict

The Special Court for Sierra Leone was established jointly by the government of Sierra Leone and the United Nations to prosecute those bearing the greatest responsibility for serious violations of international humanitarian law.

Human rights organizations welcomed the verdicts as a crucial step toward justice and accountability. The convictions sent a strong message that those who orchestrate mass atrocities would face consequences, contributing to the broader development of international criminal justice.

The RUF trial was part of the court's wider mandate, which also included the high-profile prosecution of former Liberian President Charles Taylor, who was later convicted for his role in supporting the RUF and aiding and abetting war crimes.

## Legacy

The sentencing of Sesay, Kallon, and Gbao stands as a significant milestone in efforts to address impunity for wartime atrocities. For the many survivors and victims' families in Sierra Leone, the verdicts offered a measure of justice, though the physical and psychological scars of the conflict continue to affect communities across the country.

# U.N. Special Court for Sierra Leone Delivers Justice for Wartime Atrocities

The Special Court for Sierra Leone, a hybrid tribunal established jointly by the United Nations and the Government of Sierra Leone in 2002, was created to prosecute those bearing the greatest responsibility for serious violations of international humanitarian law during the country's brutal civil war, which lasted from 1991 to 2002.

## A Decade of Conflict

Sierra Leone's civil war claimed an estimated 50,000 lives and displaced more than two million people—roughly a third of the population. Among the primary belligerents was the Revolutionary United Front (RUF), a rebel group that became notorious for its systematic campaign of terror against civilians.

## The RUF's Signature Atrocities

The RUF became internationally infamous for its practice of amputating the limbs of civilians, including women and children. These mutilations—the severing of hands, arms, and legs—were used as instruments of terror to intimidate the population and undermine support for the government. Survivors were sometimes told the amputations were a message to voters ahead of elections.

Beyond amputations, the RUF and allied factions engaged in widespread atrocities that included:

- **Recruitment of child soldiers**, often abducting children and forcing them to fight
- **Sexual violence**, including systematic rape and sexual slavery
- **Forced labor** and abductions
- **The exploitation of "blood diamonds,"** used to fund the war effort

## The Court's Work and Convictions

The Special Court indicted 13 individuals across the war's main factions, including leaders of the RUF, the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC), and the pro-government Civil Defence Forces (CDF).

Several senior RUF figures were convicted of crimes against humanity and war crimes. The court's proceedings established important legal precedents, including some of the first convictions by an international tribunal for the recruitment and use of child soldiers and for forced marriage as a crime against humanity.

## The Charles Taylor Verdict

The court's most prominent case involved **Charles Taylor**, the former President of Liberia. In April 2012, Taylor was convicted on 11 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity for aiding and abetting the RUF and other rebels, in part through the trade in blood diamonds. He was sentenced to 50 years' imprisonment.

The Taylor case marked a historic milestone: he became the first former head of state to be convicted by an international tribunal since the Nuremberg trials following World War II. Because of security concerns, his trial was held in The Hague rather than in Freetown.

## Legacy

The Special Court for Sierra Leone completed its mandate in 2013, after which a Residual Special Court was established to handle ongoing legal obligations, including the supervision of sentences and the protection of witnesses.

The tribunal is widely regarded as a significant development in international justice, demonstrating that even powerful leaders can be held accountable for atrocities. For the many survivors—including those who lost limbs to the RUF's campaign of terror—the court represented an effort to establish an official record of the crimes committed and to deliver a measure of accountability for one of Africa's most devastating conflicts.

"The Taylor case demonstrates that even those at the pinnacle of power can be brought before the law," the organization stated.

# RUF Commanders Sentenced for War Crimes in Sierra Leone Tribunal

**FREETOWN, Sierra Leone** — A UN-backed special court sentenced three former commanders of Sierra Leone's Revolutionary United Front (RUF) to lengthy prison terms in 2009 for a catalogue of atrocities committed during the country's brutal decade-long civil war, including murder, rape, sexual slavery, and forced marriage.

The Special Court for Sierra Leone handed down sentences totaling decades in prison to Issa Sesay, Morris Kallon, and Augustine Gbao, who were convicted on multiple counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Issa Sesay, who served as the RUF's interim leader in the final years of the conflict, received the harshest punishment at 52 years imprisonment. Morris Kallon, a senior battlefield commander, was sentenced to 40 years, while Augustine Gbao, who headed the RUF's security operations, received a 25-year term.

## A Landmark Ruling on Forced Marriage

Legal observers described the verdicts as historic, marking the first time an international tribunal formally recognized "forced marriage" as a distinct crime against humanity. During the war, thousands of women and girls were abducted and compelled to serve as so-called "bush wives," subjected to sexual slavery, domestic servitude, and repeated violence.

The court found that these practices constituted a separate offense from rape and sexual slavery, establishing a precedent expected to influence future international prosecutions.

## Legacy of a Brutal Conflict

Sierra Leone's civil war, which raged from 1991 to 2002, claimed an estimated 50,000 lives and displaced hundreds of thousands. The RUF became notorious for its campaign of terror, particularly the systematic hacking off of civilians' hands, arms, and legs as a tactic of intimidation. The conflict was fueled in part by the trade in so-called "blood diamonds," which financed the purchase of weapons.

The three convicted men were among the most senior RUF figures brought before the court. Prosecutors argued that they bore significant responsibility for orchestrating and enabling atrocities carried out by fighters under their command, including the widespread recruitment of child soldiers.

## Reactions

Prosecutors and human rights groups welcomed the sentences as an important step toward accountability and justice for victims. Advocates emphasized the significance of the court's recognition of gender-based crimes, which they said had too often been overlooked in international justice.

Defense attorneys had argued for leniency, with some maintaining that Sesay, in particular, had played a constructive role in the disarmament process that helped bring the war to an end.

The Special Court for Sierra Leone was established jointly by the United Nations and the government of Sierra Leone to try those bearing the greatest responsibility for atrocities committed during the conflict. The tribunal is perhaps best known for its separate, high-profile prosecution of former Liberian President Charles Taylor.

For the survivors of the war—many of them left with permanent physical and psychological scars—the sentences offered a measure of justice for crimes that shocked the world and devastated a generation.
